title: Baseball Game
description: A direct stack simulation: each operation ("C", "D", "+", or a direct score) maps one-to-one onto a basic stack operation.

blocks.text: You are keeping the scores for a baseball game with strange rules. At the beginning of the game, you start with an empty record. Given a list of strings ops, where each string represents an operation: an integer x (record a new score of x), "+" (record a new score that is the sum of the previous two scores), "D" (record a new score that is double the previous score), or "C" (invalidate/remove the previous score). Return the sum of all the scores on the record after applying all operations.

blocks.caption: A stack directly represents the running valid score record, since each operation only ever needs to look at the MOST RECENT entries

blocks.content: {"headers":["Aspect","Detail"],"rows":[["Input","An array of strings, each representing one operation"],["Output","The sum of all scores remaining on the record after all operations"],["Goal","Correctly simulate each operation, especially \"C\" (removal) and \"+\"/\"D\" (which depend on recent entries)"],["Constraints","1 <= ops.length <= 1000; ops[i] is \"C\", \"D\", \"+\", or a string representing an integer in the range [-3*10^4, 3*10^4]"]]}

{"headers":["Signal in the problem","Pattern it points to"],"rows":[["Operations depend only on the MOST RECENT entries (the last one or two scores)","A stack, since it naturally provides direct access to whatever was most recently added"],["\"C\" must UNDO the previous entry entirely","A stack's pop operation directly models \"remove the most recent entry\""]]}

blocks.text: Each operation either adds a new score directly, computes a new score based on recent scores ("+"/"D"), or removes the most recently added score entirely ("C"); the final answer is simply the sum of everything remaining.

blocks.title: Analogy: A Referee's Running Scoresheet With an "Undo" Button
blocks.text: Like a referee keeping a running scoresheet where most entries are simply written down directly, some entries are computed from the last one or two entries already written, and there is a special "undo" button that erases the most recently written entry completely, as if it never happened. A stack (a pile of paper where you can only see and remove the TOP sheet) is a natural fit for exactly this kind of running record.

blocks.caption: Each operation reads or removes only from the recent end of the stack: "C" pops, "D" doubles the top, "+" sums the top two

blocks.content: {"headers":["Operation","Stack after","Why"],"rows":[["\"5\"","[5]","Record a direct score"],["\"2\"","[5,2]","Record another direct score"],["\"C\"","[5]","Invalidate (remove) the previous score, 2"],["\"D\"","[5,10]","Double the previous score (5 * 2 = 10)"],["\"+\"","[5,10,15]","Sum of the previous two scores (5 + 10 = 15)"],["Answer","5 + 10 + 15 = 30","Sum of everything remaining on the record"]]}
{"headers":["Operation","Stack after","Why"],"rows":[["\"1\"","[1]","A single direct score"],["Answer","1","Sum of the single remaining score"]]}

blocks.text: Since every operation only ever depends on the MOST RECENTLY recorded score(s), a stack directly models the entire problem: each operation simply reads from or modifies the top of the stack.

blocks.title: Building the Intuition
blocks.text:
Observation 1: A direct number always just gets added as a new score.

Observation 2: "D" needs only the SINGLE most recent score (doubled); "+" needs the two MOST RECENT scores (summed); both are directly available as the top one or two entries of a stack.

Observation 3: "C" needs to completely remove the most recently added entry, exactly matching a stack's pop operation.

Observation 4: Since operations only ever reference the recent END of the record (never anything further back), no other data structure is needed beyond a simple stack.

Recognizing that every single operation maps DIRECTLY onto a basic stack operation (push, pop, peek) is the key simplifying insight here.
This is a direct simulation problem: process each operation in order, using a stack as the running record, since every operation only ever needs the most recent entry or entries.
Use a plain dynamic array (list) to represent the running record, applying each operation exactly as specified using standard list operations.

items: For each operation: if it is "C", remove the last score; if "D", append double the last score; if "+", append the sum of the last two scores; otherwise, parse and append the direct integer score.
Sum all remaining scores after processing every operation.

blocks.text: Why the code is written this way

items: A plain list already supports "remove the last element" and "read the last one or two elements" directly, making it functionally identical to a stack here.
This IS essentially the optimal approach already, since a list used only from one end behaves exactly like a stack.

blocks.text: Correctly simulates every operation exactly as specified, since a list accessed only from its end behaves identically to a stack.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n), a single pass through the operations (each operation is O(1)).
Space: O(n), for the record itself.

This "brute force" is effectively already optimal in this specific problem, since the natural solution already uses stack-like access exclusively; no further optimization beyond using an actual stack data structure (identical in behavior here) is meaningful.

blocks.title: The Optimization Journey
blocks.text: Since every operation naturally maps onto a basic stack operation (push a computed or direct value, or pop to undo), formalizing the "record" as an explicit stack type (rather than a general list) makes the intent of the code clearer, though the underlying behavior and complexity are identical.

Use an explicit stack. For each operation: "C" pops; "D" pushes double the current top; "+" pushes the sum of the top two (without permanently removing them from the record); any other string is parsed as a direct integer and pushed. Sum the stack at the end.
Process each operation directly against a stack, since every operation only ever needs the most recent one or two entries.

blocks.title: Final answer
blocks.text: Summing [5,-2,-4,9,5,14] gives 27, matching the expected result.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n), each operation is processed in O(1).
Space: O(n), for the stack in the worst case (no "C" operations).

Each operation is defined ENTIRELY in terms of the most recently recorded score(s), which is exactly what a stack exposes directly (its top, and the element just below it). Since no operation ever needs to reach further back into the record's history, a stack captures the full problem faithfully with no extra bookkeeping required.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Case","What happens"],"rows":[["A direct integer score","Pushed onto the stack as-is"],["\"D\"","The current top is read, doubled, and the result is pushed (the original top remains, now with the doubled value on top of it)"],["\"+\"","The top two entries are read (not removed) and their sum is pushed as a new top entry"],["\"C\"","The current top is popped (permanently removed) from the record"]]}

items: The "+" operation must NOT remove the two entries it reads, since "record a new score" means ADDING to the record, not replacing existing entries.
Care must be taken in languages where popping to read a value (as in the Java version) requires pushing it back before computing the sum, to avoid corrupting the stack's existing contents.
Summing the entire stack at the end directly answers the question, since every operation correctly maintains the stack as the exact current valid record.

blocks.text: Whenever every operation in a simulation only ever needs the MOST RECENT entry or entries (and possibly an "undo" of the most recent one), a stack is the natural and sufficient data structure, with no further optimization needed beyond recognizing this fit.

items: Accidentally REMOVING the two entries read by "+" instead of just reading them and adding a new sum entry.
Forgetting that "D" doubles the PREVIOUS score (the current top), not some fixed or unrelated value.
Mishandling the stack read-then-modify sequence for "+" in languages where peeking two levels deep is not directly supported (careful pop/push-back sequencing needed).

blocks.content: {"headers":["Edge case","Expected behavior"],"rows":[["A single direct score with no other operations","The sum is simply that one score"],["Multiple consecutive \"C\" operations","Each one removes exactly one more entry, correctly undoing multiple recent scores in sequence"],["Negative scores","Handled identically to positive ones throughout every operation"]]}

items: Recognizing (and stating) that this is a direct simulation problem, with each operation mapping one-to-one onto a basic stack operation, keeps the implementation simple and avoids overengineering.

blocks.title: If The Interviewer Says This, Think This
blocks.text: "Each operation depends only on the MOST RECENT entry/entries, plus an UNDO" points directly toward a stack-based simulation.

items: How would you extend this to support an operation that undoes the last TWO scores at once? A stack still works directly; simply pop twice for that new operation type.

What if scores needed to be looked up by an arbitrary PAST position, not just the most recent ones? A stack alone would no longer suffice; a plain indexed array (or a separate history log) would be needed instead.
How would you validate malformed input (e.g., "C" with an empty record)? Add an explicit check before popping/peeking, though the problem's constraints guarantee well-formed operation sequences here.

A straightforward simulation problem demonstrating the core stack pattern (push, pop, peek) in its most direct form, foundational to the more complex monotonic-stack problems elsewhere in this category.

blocks.title: Complexity Summary
blocks.text: Both approaches: O(n) time, O(n) space (functionally identical; the optimized version simply uses an explicit stack for clarity).

items: Pattern: Direct stack-based simulation
Core Idea: Every operation ("C", "D", "+", or a direct score) maps one-to-one onto a basic stack operation, since none of them ever need anything beyond the most recent entry or two
Time: O(n)
Space: O(n)
Most Important Observation: "+" and "D" READ recent entries without removing them, while "C" is the only operation that actually REMOVES an entry
Interview Difficulty: Easy
One-line memory trick: "C"=pop, "D"=push(top*2), "+"=push(top+second), else push(number)
